rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.e1: Attack: a fork is a move in which one piece attacks two enemy pieces at the same time, and the opponent can save only one. The knight is the forking piece par excellence: its attack cannot be blocked.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.e2: This position comes from a game played on Lichess. The black queen on h3 threatens mate on h1, and the black king is on f7. The knight on f3 has a square that reaches both.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.p: Find the knight jump that attacks the king and the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.certo: Yes, the knight on g5 makes the fork: it checks the king on f7 and, from the same square, attacks the queen on h3.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.revela: The jump is to g5: from there the knight checks the king on f7 and attacks the queen on h3 at the same time.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.err.f3e5.1: On e5 the knight captures a pawn and also gives check, but from there it does not attack the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.err.f3e5.2: With this move Black has a resource: the king steps out of check, and the queen on h3 still threatens mate on h1.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.err.f3e5.3: Back to the position: look for the square that attacks the king and the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.fora: That move does not attack the king and the queen at once. Look for a square within reach of the knight on f3 that touches both.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.volta: Try again: look for the knight jump.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.l1: With the check, Black must deal with the king before anything else, and the queen has no time to mate or to escape.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.l2: The king steps out of check to g7. No Black move saves both the king and the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.l3: The knight captures the queen on h3, and the mate threat is gone.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.l4: The rook on h8 recaptures the knight, but White has traded a knight for the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex1.l5: In positions like this, with the king and a valuable piece one jump away from the knight, the fork with check is the strongest: the opponent has no time to save the other piece.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.e1: Attack: now let us think from Black's side. A fork also works without check, against two pieces worth more than the knight or left undefended.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.e2: The white queen is on e3 and the white bishop on e5. Neither one defends the other.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.p: Find the jump of the knight on f6 that attacks the queen and the bishop.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.certo: Yes, from g4 the knight attacks the queen on e3 and the bishop on e5 at the same time.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.revela: The jump is to g4: from there the knight attacks the queen on e3 and the bishop on e5.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.fora: That move does not attack the queen and the bishop at once. Look for the square from which the knight on f6 reaches e3 and e5.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.volta: Try again: look for the jump of the knight on f6.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.l1: White must save the queen and, if possible, the bishop too, with a single move.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.l2: The queen goes to g3: it escapes, defends the bishop and even attacks the knight.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.l3: The knight captures the bishop on e5 anyway: the pawn on d6 guards e5, and if the queen recaptures, the pawn captures the queen.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.l4: In positions like this, a fork works when the opponent cannot save both pieces: no move protects both, or the defence does not hold, like the queen that cannot recapture on e5.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.err.d6e5.1: The pawn captures the bishop, but it leaves d6, and the d-file opens between the rook on d1 and your queen on d7.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.err.d6e5.2: With this move White has a resource: the rook on d1 captures the queen on d7.
rot.knightFork.ideia.ex2.err.d6e5.3: Back to the position: look for the knight square that attacks the queen and the bishop.
rot.knightFork.demos.partida.1: Attack: this position is from a Lichess game between two titled players, BahadirOzen and Seppo. The black king is on a2 and the black queen on b1, side by side.
rot.knightFork.demos.partida.2: The knight jumps to c3, defended by the bishop on e1: it checks the king on a2 and attacks the queen on b1.
rot.knightFork.demos.partida.3: The king leaves the check to b2 and attacks the knight, but the queen is still attacked.
rot.knightFork.demos.partida.4: The knight captures the queen on b1.
rot.knightFork.demos.partida.5: The king recaptures the knight: White has traded the knight for the queen.
rot.knightFork.demos.caroKann.1: Attack: this position comes from a Caro-Kann played on Lichess. The black king is on e8 and the black queen on b5. See whether the knight on e4 reaches both.
rot.knightFork.demos.caroKann.2: The knight jumps to d6: it checks the king and attacks the queen. No black piece defends d6.
rot.knightFork.demos.caroKann.3: The king leaves the check to f8, and the queen has no time to escape.
rot.knightFork.demos.caroKann.4: The knight captures the queen on b5, and no black piece can recapture.
rot.knightFork.demos.semXequeDemo.1: Attack: this position also comes from a Lichess game. Here the black king is far away, but the black queen on g6 and the black rook on f5 are one jump away from the same square.
rot.knightFork.demos.semXequeDemo.2: The knight jumps to h4, without check: it attacks the queen on g6 and the rook on f5.
rot.knightFork.demos.semXequeDemo.3: Without check, Black has a move to use: the queen escapes to g4 and attacks the knight. But the rook is left attacked.
rot.knightFork.demos.semXequeDemo.4: The knight captures the rook on f5.
rot.knightFork.demos.semXequeDemo.5: The queen recaptures the knight, but White has traded a knight for a rook. In positions like this, a fork without check wins material even when the opponent saves the more valuable piece.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.1: Attack: this position also comes from a Lichess game. The knight on b5 has two jumps with check to the king on e8, to d6 and to c7. Which of them is the fork that works?
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.2: The jump to d6 checks the king and attacks the bishop on c8. It looks like a fork.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.3: But the bishop on f8 guards d6 and captures the knight. Here the fork does not work, and White just loses the knight.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.4: Back to the position: before the fork, check who guards the target square. If the defender captures the knight for free, the fork does not work; if the knight is defended too, as on e5 in the example with Black, the defender cannot capture without losing.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.5: On c7 no black piece guards the square: the knight gives check and attacks the rook on a8.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.6: The king leaves the check to d7, and the rook on a8 is still attacked.
rot.knightFork.demos.excecao.7: The knight captures the rook on a8.
rot.knightFork.pratica.valeAqui.enunciad: The knight on b5 can jump to c7, with check and an attack on the rook on a8. Does the fork work here? Check who guards each square and play as White.
rot.knightFork.pratica.valeAqui.fim: On c7 the fork did not work. On d6 the knight gave check and attacked the bishop on b7, and the queen on c5 could not take it, because the rook on d1 guards d6.
rot.knightFork.pratica.valeAqui.err.d1d6: The rook captures the pawn on d6, but there it is attacked by the queen on c5, and Black gets the better game. Look for the knight jump that makes the fork that works.
rot.knightFork.pratica.valeAqui.err.b5c7: With the jump to c7 you give up the knight: the queen on c5 guards that square and captures it.
rot.knightFork.pratica.slav.enunciado: Now let us think from Black's side. The pawn on a3 attacks your knight on b4. Play as Black and find the best move.
rot.knightFork.pratica.slav.fim: Instead of retreating, the knight jumped to c2, checking the king and attacking the rook on a1, and won the rook.
rot.knightFork.pratica.slav.err.b4d3: With the check on d3 you give up the knight: the pawn on e2 captures it.
rot.knightFork.pratica.slav.err.b4c6: Retreating saves the knight, but it has a stronger jump that attacks two pieces.
rot.knightFork.pratica.slav.err.b4a6: Retreating saves the knight, but it has a stronger jump that attacks two pieces.
rot.knightFork.pratica.semXeque.enunciad: Back to White. Here the black king is far from your knight. Play as White and find the best move.
rot.knightFork.pratica.semXeque.fim: On e6 the knight attacked the queen on d8 and the rook on f8 without check: the queen escaped, and the knight captured the rook.
rot.knightFork.pratica.semXeque.err.f4e2: The knight retreats to e2 and attacks no black piece. Look for the square from which it attacks the queen and the rook.
rot.knightFork.pratica.semXeque.err.f4d5: On d5 the knight does not attack two pieces: the knight on f6 takes it, and the knights are simply traded. Look for the square that reaches the queen and the rook.
